prompt: An in-order core has base CPI 1.0. Every instruction is fetched from L1i (miss rate 1%), and 30% of instructions access data in L1d (miss rate 6%). Base CPI includes cache hits. Assume blocking execution with no overlapping miss penalties; each miss adds 60 cycles. What is the effective CPI?

options.explanation: 1.68 is the stall component alone. The base CPI of 1.0 must be added.
This counts the data-miss stalls (0.3 × 0.06 × 60 = 1.08) but leaves out instruction-fetch misses.
Correct. Instruction-fetch misses add 1 × 0.01 × 60 = 0.6 cycles per instruction and data misses add 0.3 × 0.06 × 60 = 1.08, so the total is 1.0 + 0.6 + 1.08 = 2.68 cycles per instruction.
This applies the 6% data miss rate to every instruction (1 × 0.06 × 60 = 3.6) instead of only the 30% that access data, and also leaves out the instruction-fetch stalls: 1.0 + 3.6 = 4.6.

workedExample:
For a blocking core with non-overlapping misses, each kind of memory reference adds its own stall cycles per instruction, and they sum on top of the base CPI:

```formula
CPI = CPI_base + S_I + S_D
S_I = r_I m_I t_penalty
S_I = 1.0 × 0.01 × 60 = 0.60
S_D = r_D m_D t_penalty
S_D = 0.3 × 0.06 × 60 = 1.08
CPI = 1.0 + 0.60 + 1.08 = 2.68
where
CPI: cycles per instruction: the average clock cycles each instruction takes, here including memory stalls
CPI_base: CPI with perfect caches, hits included: 1.0
S_I: stall cycles per instruction from instruction-fetch misses
r_I: instruction fetches per instruction: 1.0, every instruction is fetched
m_I: the L1i (instruction cache) miss rate, 1% = 0.01
t_penalty: the extra cycles each miss costs, 60
S_D: stall cycles per instruction from data misses
r_D: data accesses per instruction: 30% = 0.3
m_D: the L1d (data cache) miss rate, 6% = 0.06
In words: instruction misses add 0.6 cycles and data misses 1.08 cycles to every instruction, so the 1.0 base becomes 2.68.
```

So the machine runs 2.68× slower than with perfect caches. An out-of-order design may hide some penalties if sufficient independent work exists; its actual CPI is not determined by this model.

prompt: A blocking, non-overlapping miss-penalty model predicts 30 stall cycles per 100 instructions, but an out-of-order execution measures less. Which explanations are plausible? Select all that apply.

options.text: The core overlaps several independent misses (memory-level parallelism), so their latencies are not paid one after another
options.explanation: Correct. Independent requests can overlap if sufficient tracking capacity and bandwidth are available. The number of outstanding requests is implementation-dependent.

options.text: Independent instructions execute while a miss is outstanding, hiding part of its latency
options.explanation: Correct. Out-of-order execution keeps doing useful work until the reorder buffer fills or a dependent instruction is needed.

options.text: Hardware prefetchers turn some predicted misses into hits or partial hits
options.explanation: Correct. Prefetched lines arrive early or are already in flight when the demand load comes.

options.text: AMAT ignores the hit time, so it always overestimates
options.explanation: AMAT explicitly includes the hit time. The overestimate comes from assuming misses are serial and fully exposed.

options.text: Out-of-order cores have no L1 cache misses
options.explanation: Out-of-order execution does not eliminate cache misses. It can change their timing and hide some penalties; identical miss counts are not guaranteed.

workedExample: AMAT is average service time per access in its stated model, not automatically total stall CPI. A non-overlapping stall model adds only extra miss penalties to hit/base execution costs. Real execution can overlap independent misses, do useful work while waiting, or benefit from prefetches absent from the model. Queueing and bandwidth limits also matter, so AMAT alone does not reliably rank every real design.
